Problem: what comes next? What do you think the next word (token) will be? I want to eat some delicious ____ Likely: food ("roti", "sushi") Unlikely: "trucks", "schedules", ... People know this from experience. Can we give machines an approximation of this? Less informally: Construct a model to compute the probability of a token sequence, [ w0, w1, ..., wn ] and assess how natural it is.

Language model Definition : An assignment of probability to a sequence of words* We want P(w1, w2, ..., wn) Can be used to predict next word* in sequence, ala P(next_word | previous_words) "Grammatical and fluent" sequences get higher probability than "word salad" Broad use in NLP tasks: autocomplete / autocorrect, speech recognition, fluency in machine translation, etc. We don't want: *

A corpus: two lies and a truth I like cats I like dogs I hate rain

Basic probability (reminder + NLP) I like cats I like dogs I hate rain Notation Example: corpus above Sample space (Ω): all possible outcomes { cats, dogs, hate, like, I, rain } P(Ω) = 1 Only words { cats, dogs, ..., rain } Event (A): any event in the sample space "like" is written (spoken?) P(A): how likely A is (0.0 < P(A) < 1.0) P("like") = 2/9 Events can take any letter / name: A, B, ...

Unigram language model Using basic probability: P(token) = count(token) / N I like cats I like dogs I hate rain P(sentence1) = P(w1, w2, w3) = 0.3333 * 0.2222 * 0.1111 = 0.008 Token Count Probability cats 1 1 / 9 = 0.1111 dogs 1 1 / 9 = 0.1111 hate 1 1 / 9 = 0.1111 I 3 3 / 9 = 0.3333 like 2 2 / 9 = 0.2222 rain 1 1 / 9 = 0.1111

Unigram language model uses Unigram language models can be used in detecting depression, etc. Eg. Chung & Pennebaker (2007): Focus on "function" words & ignore everything else This is surprising for obvious reasons (eg. not as useful to focus on affective words General problem with unigram models Sequences / sentences with identical probability scores: A hair I my to twice used wash week I used to wash my hair twice a week Unigram models cannot determine grammatical & fluent language Conclusion: unigram language models should be used sparingly

Joint probability (reminder) Fixing the unigram LM Probability that two events occur We need better probabilities to make the model sensitive to order Start with bigrams: 2-token sequences For this, we need joint probability A A∩B B Call events: A and B Probability of A and B both occurring Joint probability: Easy to calculate with dice, cards, etc. Harder to calculate with language P(A,B) = P(A∩B)

Chain rule of joint probability From one event to many (possible) events with conditional probability P(A, B) = P(A) × P(B|A) A longer joint probability can be calculated from a product of conditionals P(A, B, C) = P(A) × P(B|A) × P(C|A,B) ... and this holds for any number of events P(A1,...,An) = P(A1) × P(A2|A1) × P(A3|A1,A2) × ... × P(An|A1,...,An−1)

Conditional probability We can get to joint probability through conditional probability Probability of one event given we know another event has occurred Example 1: I like cats I like dogs I hate rain A A∩B B Given the corpus What is the probability observing "like" given that "I" is observed? Example 2: Given the corpus What is the probability observing "dogs" given that "hate" is observed? P(A|B) = P(A∩B) / P(B)

The chain rule applied to sentences Calculating the probability of a sentence of length n P(w n1, ..., w n) = P(w 1) x P(w 2|w1) x P(w 3|w1,w2) x ... x P(w n|w1, ..., w n-1) This formula will give us the exact probability ... IF the sentence appears in the training corpus ... but will not give us estimates for anything not seen before (eg. "I hate cats") We need an approximate history

The Markov assumption Assume the next token depends only on the last k tokens A simplifying approximation It's not true for long-distance dependencies, eg. "I will pick the coffee up" ... but it trades a little accuracy for tractability Model History size Formula Context / Note Unigram k=0 P(wi) Ignores context entirely Bigram k=1 P(wi | wi-1) One token context Trigram k=2 P(wi | wi-2, wi-1) Two tokens context n-gram k = 0, 1, ... P(wi | wi-3, wi-2, wi-1) No special names beyond trigram; Context = n-1;

Bigram probability estimates First: useful to introduce two new symbols to our corpus <s> I like cats </s> <s> I like dogs </s> <s> I hate rain </s> Next, we can determine counts of all 2-word sequences Afterwards, we can use the counts for maximum likelihood estimation <s> = start of sequence / sentence </s> = end of sequence / sentence An estimate of a probability based on relative frequency in the corpus MLE = occurrence / sum(context) We can use MLE estimates to determine sentence probabilities

Problem: nothing like that, please Keep abusive language out of my DMs ... and put spam in its own folder

Classifying language A language model can be used to classify language Example: abusive language Example: spam filter This is also a conditional probability Example: the word "pay" You see a lot of spam messages with "pay" — eg. "we pay for your opinion" You also have an occasional message from your employer with "net pay" You can construct a system to classify messages based on unigram probabilities: P(spam|"pay") = P("pay" | spam) · P(spam) / P("pay") This determines a hard-to-know quantity (class given tokens) using an easy-to-determine quantity (word given class) This is an application of Bayes' Rule
Bayes' Rule The degree to which the model predicts the data Likelihood Prior How probable is the hypothesis? Posterior Normalization Constant Probabilities must sum to 1.0
Problem: evidence of the unseen I have a corpus Give me the probability of a sentence using the corpus

Problem, with some detail We can estimate sentence probabilities for items already seen Markov assumption: look in a small (n-gram) window Maximum likelihood estimation: establish counts from n-grams in corpus N-gram models break with unseen events Example, given the corpus we used before → We may have unseen but plausible patterns I like cats I like dogs I hate rain I like rain We may have unseen but plausible word types I love my suitcase Some events have zero probability in the n-gram language models

Perplexity (PP), a metric Definition : the inverse probability of the test set, normalised by the number of words, N, for a (test) word sequence W = { w1, w2, ..., wN } General formula Special case for bigram models Given training set ("cats, etc") and test set ("rain") what is P("rain" | "like")? I like cats I like dogs I hate rain I like rain

Perplexity intuition Narrative: Lower PP score = higher probability assigned to test set = better model The average number of equally-likely words the model has to choose from at any step Perplexity of 10 means that every time the model tries to predict the next word, it is as confused as if it were choosing among 10 equally-likely words Best practices We must smooth the language model — account for unseen types and combinations Low perplexity scores do not guarantee good performance on NLP tasks Measure perplexity on "held out" (previously-unseen) data

Robin Hood principle (smoothing) Robin Hood steals from the rich and give to the poor Concept: smoothing Take probability mass from existing n-grams Add probability mass to unseen n-grams to make everything at least slightly possible Before smoothing After smoothing 0.5 0.43 0.35 0.31 0.15 seen A seen B seen C 0.14 unseen seen A seen B seen C 0.12 unseen No scruffiness We can just assign some probability to these zero-probability events But because we're dealing with probabilities, the approach must be principled

Laplace ("add 1") smoothing Concept: How many n-grams should there be? Example: if there are 6 types in the corpus, estimate there should be 6 more Add 1 to each observed count I like cats Add V (size of vocab) to normalise properly Applies to n-grams of every n General formula I like dogs I hate rain

More vocab, more problems V (context size) is often large — 10K+ items is reasonable — and this becomes a problem Adding |V| to every denominator makes seen n-grams MUCH less likely — especially true for contexts with few observations Result: Laplace smoothing aggressively overcorrects It assigns too much probability mass to unseen events It steals too much from observed events Real systems need "gentler" smoothing

Add-k smoothing Together with Laplace, this is generally called additive smoothing Instead of adding 1, add "k" 0<k<1 Exact value is a hyperparameter Formula With k = 0.1, determine the probabilities for the following bigrams: <s> I I like I hate I rain ti-1 \ ti </s> cats dogs hate I <s> rain 3 I like like 1 1 1 2

Hyperparameters / holding out for k Hyperparameters are values set before training starts Different values of "k" result in different overall performance We want to tune all hyperparameters to yield the best performance What is the ideal value for k? We know that 0 < k < 1 The ideal value depends on the data (i.e. may be different on different corpora / datasets) Generally, we use a data-driven approach: Split the data into 3 sets: train, valid, test Train/validation cycle: Train a model on "train" data using a value of k Test the performance of the model on valid data Repeat "train/validation cycle for several values of k Train data Corpus / dataset Build the model Validation data Determine hyperparam values Test data Model performance

The problem with Add-k Not all events are likely Some events with the same add-k probability shouldn't Example: In the counts, should an empty cell ("like" x "rain") be "worth more" than a missing cell? OOV → <UNK> Previously unseen types are "out of vocabulary" (OOV) Need to attach a probability to unseen unigrams as well These don't exist for some problems (eg. closed vocabulary tasks, selecting from a menu) I like faquig → I like <UNK> Typical solution: During testing: replace all OOV items with a special token "<UNK>" during testing During training: replace least common types with "<UNK>" tokens

Backoff & Interpolation Backoff models N-gram was never observed ? backoff to the (n-1)-gram If the trigram was never seen, fall back to the bigram estimate If the bigram was never seen, fall back to the unigram estimate Always use the highest-order estimate available Interpolation Always blend the model orders: p(n-gram) = λ1 * p(unigram) + λ2 * p(bigram) + λ3 * p(trigram) Learn λ values on a validation set ... and ensure sum(λi) is 1.0 Interpolation is generally more robust than backoff

NLP techniques when at scale Prune models Remove low-frequency words / n-grams Zipf's distribution implies: cut off rare events Find threshold through held-out dataset? Efficiency Use efficient data structures, like tries Use Bloom filters (for approximate LMs) Use approximate (scruffy?) algorithms — eg. Summary A language model is an assignment of probability to a word sequence A good language model allows us to determine / generate grammatical & fluent language We often make a Markov assumption and build LMs from smaller n-grams We may be able to use LMs to classify sentences, utterances or other language Smoothing A language model needs to be smoothed to account for unseen events Perplexity Allows us to compare different language models Better performance (lower perplexity scores) result from higher probability for grammatical & fluent language We have a number of smoothing approaches of increasing complexity (Laplace, Add-k, Backoff, Interpolation, Good-Turing, Absolute Discounting, Kneser-Ney)

Naive Bayes Naive Bayes A general-purpose classifier from machine learning "Naive" because the algorithm assumes a word's probability is independent of other words in the same class Independence assumption is obviously incorrect Document: A sequence of words (tokens) P(document|class) is a joint probability over the word sequence Assume a bag-of-words (unigram) model Example: a document with the word "prize" is more likely to contain "win".

Problem: it works ... only sometimes You've built a Naive Bayes classifier It works well if the language is simple It fails on negations, multi-word expressions, etc.

Naive Bayes classifier works Bayesian classifiers are great at some things: They are fast and simple to implement They provide a robust performance for a lot of tasks The independence assumption has a cost Word combinations are assumed to be completely independent, eg.: The movie was solid. This will be seen as positive The negativity will be down-weighted Generally, multi-word expressions may confuse Bayesian models The movie was not solid. 1 0

A classifier of a different colour Naive Bayes A generative classifier Models P(document|class) and P(class) then combines them with Bayes' rule Implicitly models how a document of each class was generated Needs the independence assumption to stay tractable Logistic Regression A discriminative classifier Models P(class|document) directly — no detour through P(document|class) Does not try to explain how the document was created, only how to tell classes apart Free to use arbitrary, overlapping or correlated features

Complexity Essentially, logistic regression tries to: Define a line according to a bias & some feature weights Bend a line (using sigmoid) to fit a probability curve Measure distance to best-fitting model using BCELoss or similar The line has a lot of parameters — feature weights (θ vector) + 1 The closed-form ("using a formula") solution may have running time: Step Running time Compute XTX O(n|θ|2) Compute XTy O(n|θ|) Solve the d d system O(n|θ|3) Overall O(n|θ|2 + |θ|3)

We prefer gradient descent Idea: Measure how "wrong" the θ hypothesis is Take a fractional step (0 < α < 1) in the right direction to improve Converge when θ updates are within some threshold ε Algorithm θ ← randomly or 0s; check: 0 < α < 1; check: ε >= 0 # Initialise repeat until convergence: ∇J (gradient of cost function) = compute_gradient(X, Y, θ) θ_new = θ - α * ∇J if ||θ_new - θ|| < ε or ||∇J|| < ε: convergence = True else: θ = θ_new This may be the most important algorithm in machine learning

Precision and recall Precision Recall Of everything classified as spam, how much was actually spam? Of all the actual spam, how much did the model catch? Low precision → a lot of "false alarms" (real mail getting blocked). Low recall → too much spam slipping into the inbox

F1 score (F-score?) Combines precision and recall Precision = quality of prediction Recall = completeness of prediction F1 is the "harmonic mean" between the two Weights toward the lower of the two scores Calculations F1 score Recall % -orPrecision %
